solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Game stats an academic partly recalled

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters found are read back the other way
only part of the run of words 'stats an academic' is wanted, so the answer sits inside them

parts.note: the letters running across statS AN ACademic

explanation.surface: A statistician's figures on some game are dug up and quoted again.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards through 'stATS AN ACademic' and CANASTA appears; 'Game' looks like it qualifies 'stats' but stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Canasta is a rummy-style card game played with two packs, so it is one example of a game.

clue.text: Teams reportedly avoid isle when dropping second bomb

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, so the abbreviation for 'second' falls out of the phrase
'reportedly' means as it is said out loud, so the word for 'Teams' is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: crews are teams, as on a ship or film set
s = second, the unit of time; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: A sports team, hearing a bomb is coming, dodges an island as it is dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: The S that falls out is the one belonging to the island, leaving a word for a projectile. 'Second' looks like an ordinal but is the unit abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A cruise missile is a guided, low-flying weapon carrying a warhead, loosely a kind of bomb.

clue.text: Figure in lane drunk with rum

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so the letters of 'lane' and 'rum' are jumbled

explanation.surface: A figure is spotted in the lane, drunk on rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' reads as a person staggering down a lane; it is the definition, meaning a written number.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure is a written symbol standing for a number, which is exactly what a numeral is.

clue.text: Claim implicates very old Alpine region

indicators.note: to implicate is to fold something in, so 'Claim' wraps around the letters for 'very old'

parts.note: to say so is to claim it

explanation.surface: An accusation drags an ancient mountain district into trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: V and O go inside SAY. 'Implicates' reads as an accusation in the surface but here only means enfolds.
explanation.definitionFit: Savoy is a historic mountainous territory in the western Alps, now split between France and Italy.

clue.text: When on top, boss uncovered insulator

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sitting on another is placed above it, so 'When' goes first

parts.note: as = when, as in 'as I left'
to top a rival is to best them

indicators.note: stripped of its covering, 'boss' loses its first and last letters and keeps only its middle

explanation.surface: Once the boss is in charge, he is revealed as a cold, insulated figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' and 'boss' both look like nouns for a leader; 'top' is the verb meaning to beat.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestos is a fibrous mineral once widely used to block heat and fire, a classic insulating material.

clue.text: PM following officers in alarm

indicators.note: one thing following another comes after it, so the Prime Minister is placed after the officers

parts.note: DIs are Detective Inspectors, police officers

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister tails a group of officials in a state of panic.
explanation.walkthrough: PM is the Prime Minister, not the afternoon; Theresa May was British Prime Minister from 2016 to 2019.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismay and alarm are both nouns for sudden distress or consternation at bad news.

clue.text: Result of tots consuming last of Brie?

definitions.text: Result of tots consuming last of Brie?

indicators.note: to consume is to take in, so 'tots' swallows the final letter of 'Brie'

parts.note: tots and drams are small measures of spirits

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Small children eating cheese at bedtime: what happens next?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tots' looks like toddlers but means small drinks. The whole clue also defines: cheese before bed is said to bring vivid dreams.
explanation.definitionFit: Folklore holds that eating cheese late at night causes vivid visions in sleep, so these are its result.

clue.text: Trifling matter upset large male Serb

indicators.note: upset things are knocked out of their order, so the letters after it are rearranged

parts.note: l = large, as on clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A big Serbian man is upset over some trivial matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like it describes the Serb's mood; it acts on the letters. 'Large' is reduced to its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Small beer is an idiom for something unimportant, from the weak ale once drunk everyday.

clue.text: Poison retired artist initially seen cycling city

indicators.note: retiring is drawing back, so the letters for 'artist' go the other way
cycling round means the city's letters rotate, the front one moving to the back

parts.note: RA = Royal Academician, the usual crossword artist

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of 'seen' is kept

parts.note: Nice, the city on the French Riviera

explanation.surface: A retired painter was seen bicycling round a city with poison.
explanation.walkthrough: NICE rotated by one letter becomes ENIC, the N moving to the end. 'Cycling' reads as a bike ride but tells you to rotate.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenic is a chemical element whose compounds are notoriously toxic, the classic poisoner's choice.

clue.text: Fast blue van possibly patrolling edges of Monaco

indicators.note: a patrol goes all round an area, so the jumbled letters surround the Monaco pair
'possibly' offers one of the forms the letters of 'blue van' could take
the edges of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A speedy blue police van patrols the boundaries of Monaco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' reads as speedy, which suits a patrol van; here it is the other sense, firmly fixed, as in 'stuck fast'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast can mean firmly fixed in place, as in 'held fast', which is being immovable.

clue.text: Famous Greek model turned on American

indicators.note: turned round means facing the other way, so the joined pieces read backwards
'on' means next to, so the American abbreviation is joined after 'model'

parts.note: to model is to pose for an artist

explanation.surface: A celebrated Greek fashion model has fallen for an American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' looks like a phrasal verb about attraction; it splits into a reversal indicator and a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek storyteller credited with the well-known collection of animal fables.

clue.text: Penny on front desk adopting fool's earlier idea

indicators.note: in a down clue 'on' puts the penny above what follows
to adopt is to take in, so 'front desk' takes in the word for 'fool'

parts.note: the reception is the front desk of a hotel or office

explanation.surface: Someone called Penny, at the front desk, takes on a fool's earlier plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny' looks like a receptionist's name; it is just P. The apostrophe-s on 'fool' is the link between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A preconception is a notion formed beforehand, before evidence arrives, so an idea held in advance.

clue.text: Beam attached to rear of stone range

indicators.note: fixed to the back of something means placed after it, so the beam follows the stone

parts.note: st = stone, the British unit of weight
a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: A timber beam is fixed to the back of a stone cooking range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rear of stone' tempts you to take its last letter E; the whole abbreviation ST goes before the beam. A stone is 14 pounds, a British weight.
explanation.definitionFit: To range and to stray both mean to wander about freely, over a wide area.

clue.text: Appearance of Mabel oddly in spirited meeting

indicators.note: one thing put in another sits inside it, so the chosen letters go inside the meeting

parts.note: a seance is a sitting to contact spirits

indicators.note: oddly picks out the odd-numbered letters of the name, first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: Mabel turns up at a lively gathering, looking rather odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirited' reads as lively, but a meeting with spirits is a seance.
explanation.definitionFit: Semblance means the outward look or show of something, a synonym for appearance.

clue.text: Note bird seizing delicate hollow instrument

parts.note: me (or mi) is the third note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: to seize is to grab hold of, so the bird wraps round the emptied word

parts.note: a loon is a diver, a water bird

indicators.note: a hollow word has had its inside scooped out, leaving only its outer letters

explanation.surface: A bird grabs a fragile, hollow musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hollow instrument' reads as one phrase, like a drum; 'hollow' belongs with 'delicate', and 'instrument' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A melodeon is a small button accordion or reed organ, one particular musical instrument.

clue.text: Ship's orders yet to be broadcast

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters seed widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: A ship's commands have not yet gone out over the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'is', linking 'Ship' to the anagram; the surface reads it as possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A destroyer is a fast, lightly armoured warship, one specific kind of naval vessel.

clue.text: Material against the Spanish crown twice abridged

indicators.note: abridging shortens a word, and doing it twice cuts two letters from the end of 'crown'

parts.note: CROWN loses its last two letters

explanation.surface: A document opposing the Spanish monarchy, cut down twice by the censors.
explanation.walkthrough: V for versus is the standard abbreviation for 'against', as in sport and law cases.
explanation.definitionFit: Velcro is a trademarked hook-and-loop fastening fabric, a particular kind of material.

clue.text: Came in to view parrot circling fruit close to shed

indicators.note: circling something goes all round it, so the word for 'parrot' surrounds the fruit

parts.note: to parrot or ape is to mimic

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the last letter of 'shed' is kept

explanation.surface: Someone stepped inside to look at a parrot flying round some fruit near a shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parrot' looks like a bird but is the verb to copy.
explanation.definitionFit: To come into view and to appear both mean to become visible, both here in the past tense.

clue.text: Most tender son covering female in wooded area

indicators.note: covering something hides it and takes its place, so the son stands in for the female

parts.note: s = son, as in family trees
f = female; this letter is replaced
a forest is a large wooded area

explanation.surface: A gentle son shields a woman in the woods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most tender' reads as loving; it means most painful. F in FOREST is swapped for S.
explanation.definitionFit: Tender can mean painful to the touch, like a bruise, so the most tender spot is the most sore.

clue.text: Jammed on piano before time within shelter

indicators.note: something within another is inside it, so 'time' goes inside 'shelter'
one thing before another comes first, so the piano is placed ahead of the shelter

parts.note: the lee is the sheltered side

explanation.surface: Someone played the piano in a jam session before taking shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jammed on piano' reads as a musical jam; 'on' is a separate piece meaning concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: Replete means filled to capacity or stuffed full, which is being jammed or packed.

clue.text: Isolated harvests bordering 60% of Idaho to the west

indicators.note: sixty per cent of a five-letter word is three letters, so the rest of the state is cut
in an across clue west is leftward, so the whole assembly reads right to left
to border something is to run along both sides of it, so 'harvests' surrounds the shortened state

parts.note: the first three of IDAHO's five letters

explanation.surface: Scattered farm harvests run along part of Idaho's western edge.
explanation.walkthrough: The state goes inside the crops after the first letter, and only then does everything turn round. 'To the west' passes for geography in an Idaho surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporadic means occurring here and there or now and then, scattered, as isolated cases are.

clue.text: See European code is cracked

indicators.note: something cracked is broken apart, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Look: the European code has been broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' opens the clue like an imperative, look; it is the noun, a bishop's seat, as in the Holy See.
explanation.definitionFit: A see is the district under a bishop's authority, which is a diocese.

clue.text: Marine creature contractor delivered?

indicators.note: a speech is delivered out loud, so the word for 'contractor' is heard, not spelt

parts.note: a muscle is a contractor, working by contracting

explanation.surface: A builder has delivered some kind of sea creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contractor' looks like a builder; it is anything that contracts, here a muscle.
explanation.definitionFit: A mussel is a bivalve shellfish living on sea rocks, so a creature of the sea.

clue.text: Setter's left with a French press

parts.note: the setter is I, so 'setter's' is I'm, I am
port is the left side of a ship
une is 'a' in French; 'with' just joins it on

explanation.surface: The crossword setter has gone off with a French printing press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter's' is I'm, the setter speaking of themself. 'Press' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To importune is to beg or urge someone persistently, which is to press them.

clue.text: Shares withdrawn to get sailing vessel

indicators.note: withdrawing is pulling back, so the word for 'shares' goes backwards

parts.note: to share resources is to pool them

explanation.surface: An investor pulls shares out of the market to buy a yacht.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shares' and 'withdrawn' sound like the stock market; 'shares' is the verb, as in pooling resources.
explanation.definitionFit: A sloop is a single-masted sailboat with one headsail, a particular kind of sailing boat.

clue.text: Southern college welcomes northern Muslim

indicators.note: welcoming a guest means taking them in, so 'college' takes in the letter for 'northern'

explanation.surface: A college in the south opens its doors to a Muslim student from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Southern' is not a place label here; its initial S leads the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunni is the largest branch of Islam, and the word also names an adherent, a Muslim of that branch.

clue.text: Refined colonist released unknown song

indicators.note: once released, the colonist has been let go, so that word is removed from 'Refined'

parts.note: ants live in colonies; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A cultured settler, freed at last, sings of the unknown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colonist' suggests a settler; in crosswords it is usually an ant. ELEGANT without ANT is ELEG.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a mournful poem or piece of music, a lament, so loosely a song.

clue.text: African protected area in new green site

indicators.note: a new version is a remade one, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wildlife reserve in Africa sits on a fresh green site.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits: a nature reserve is a green site.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti is a Tanzanian national park and ecosystem famous for wildlife migration, a protected reserve.

clue.text: Skin around wings of taller seabird

indicators.note: going around something encloses it, so the word for 'skin' surrounds the letters from 'taller'
the wings of a word are its two sides, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A taller seabird's wings are wrapped in skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wings' suits a seabird but means the outside letters of 'taller'.
explanation.definitionFit: Petrels are tube-nosed ocean birds such as the storm petrel, a family of seabirds.

clue.text: A lot of blether in front of home cinema?

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the word loses its last letter
one piece in front of another comes first, so the talk precedes the word for 'home'

parts.note: DRIVEL, nonsense talk, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: Lots of chatter in front of the home cinema screen.
explanation.walkthrough: Blether is Scots and northern British for foolish talk, the same as drivel. The question mark flags that a drive-in is one kind of cinema.
explanation.definitionFit: A drive-in is an open-air cinema where the audience watches films from their parked cars.
